Platforms and auctions: two markets where the rule makes the result
The world’s largest companies are often platforms, and many things are sold at auction, from ad slots to Swedish flats. In both cases, the answer depends on a rule: who pays what, and who sees what.

L14 (Friberg 18.1–18.3): platforms (two-sided markets), pricing, concentration; auctions (formats, private or common values, revenue equivalence). Exam links: platforms E2022, E2025; auctions E2023, E2025.
A platform: two groups meeting through an intermediary

A stock exchange, a dating app, a free ad-funded newspaper, a credit card, an operating system: each time, two groups use the same intermediary, and what one group does changes the value for the other.

L14: a platform (two-sided or multi-sided market) brings together 1) two sets of agents who interact through an intermediary and 2) decisions on one side that affect the other. Types: exchanges, matchmaking, ad-supported media, transaction systems, software platforms.
Without the second criterion, a simple reseller would be a platform: it is the cross effects that change pricing.
Platform design aims to foster positive effects (reviews, sharing) and limit negative ones (moral hazard, adverse selection, trolls, congestion).

A platform charges little, or even subsidises, the side whose demand is elastic and which creates a lot of value for the other: its effective cost is c_b minus the value it brings to sellers. In a private-value second-price auction, my bid decides whether I win but the best rival sets the payment; bidding my value is weakly dominant. In a first-price auction, my bid is my payment: I bid below my value. With a common value, winning signals that I was the most optimistic, hence the winner’s curse.
